name: Venice
info: Venice is a city on a group of islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic in north-eastern Italy, traditionally founded in 421, and for almost a thousand years the capital of a maritime republic.

facts.founded: Traditionally on 25 March 421, with the dedication of the church of San Giacomo at Rialto; no surviving records deal with the founding, and the first settlers are held to have been refugees from Roman cities of the mainland
facts.where: On a group of islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, between the mouths of the Po and the Piave, in the Veneto region of north-eastern Italy
facts.known: The Republic of Venice and its doges; the Arsenal; the Fourth Crusade; the printing press of Aldus Manutius; Venetian painting; Murano glass; the Ghetto; the lagoon and its canals
facts.today: Venice is the capital of the Veneto region and of the Metropolitan City of Venice, and its lagoon and historic centre are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

t: Venice grew from lagoon communities of fishermen and refugees under the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna into an independent republic whose ducal seat moved to Rialto in the early 9th century.
Its fleets, its trade with Constantinople and the Levant and its share of the Byzantine lands after 1204 made it, by the late 13th century, the most prosperous city in Europe.
The sea route round the Cape of Good Hope, the Ottoman wars and the plagues wore its power down, and Napoleon ended the Republic in May 1797.
dyk: The word ghetto is originally Venetian: it names the area of Venice in which Jews were compelled to live under the Republic.
ev: Tradition dates the founding to the dedication of the church of San Giacomo on the islet of Rialto
Pepin of Italy withdraws after a six-month siege of the lagoon, in which his army is ravaged by disease
Relics claimed to be those of St Mark the Evangelist are brought from Alexandria to the new basilica
Venetians and French crusaders capture and sack Constantinople, and Venice takes territories in the Aegean, including Crete
The Venetians destroy the Genoese fleet at the Battle of Chioggia
Venice is defeated at Agnadello by the League of Cambrai and recovers its mainland lands over the next seven years
Plague kills about a third of the population
Napoleon conquers Venice and the Republic ends, and the city passes to Austria by the Treaty of Campo Formio

sections.origins:
Venice stands on a group of islands in the shallow Venetian Lagoon, an enclosed bay at the head of the Adriatic between the mouths of the Po and the Piave. The islands rest on alluvial silt washed down from the Alps. No surviving historical records deal directly with the founding or building of the city. Tradition and the available evidence have led several historians to agree that the first population was made up of refugees from nearby Roman cities such as Padua, Aquileia, Treviso, Altinum and Concordia, and from the undefended countryside, who were fleeing successive Germanic and Hun invasions. Late Roman sources mention fishermen on the islands, called incolae lacunae, "lagoon dwellers".

The traditional founding is the dedication of the church of San Giacomo on the islet of Rialto (Rivoalto, "High Shore"), said to have taken place at noon on 25 March 421. One account adds that authorities from Padua founded the city as a trading post. The church itself is dated no earlier than the 11th century and no later than the mid-12th, so the date remains a tradition. Archaeology shows that the island of Olivolo, now San Pietro di Castello, was inhabited in the 5th century, and the Rialto islands were not properly urbanised until the 9th. The settlers learned to build by driving closely spaced alder piles into the mud and sand until they reached compressed clay, and laid plates of Istrian limestone on top.
sections.growth:
From the 9th to the 12th century Venice developed into a maritime power, one of the Italian maritime republics. Its position at the head of the Adriatic made its naval and commercial strength almost invulnerable, and its reliable gold ducat supported confidence in its trade. Early prosperity probably owed much to a trade in slaves taken in central Europe and sold to North Africa and the Levant. In the 12th century the Republic built a large shipyard, the Arsenal, which several historians regard as the first factory in history. After 1204 it held Crete, Euboea and the islands of the Duchy of the Archipelago. It dominated the trade in salt and was a centre of commerce in silk, grain and spice.

By the late 13th century Venice was the most prosperous city in Europe. At the peak of its power, in 1410, it had a navy of some 3,300 ships manned by 36,000 men. Its population was 60,000 in 1000, 80,000 in 1200 and between 110,000 and 180,000 in 1300, about 170,000 in the mid-1500s and close to 200,000 by 1600. The guilds produced silks, brocades, goldsmith work, armour and glass. By 1500 the city had 417 printers, and the Aldine Press of Aldus Manutius, founded in 1494, printed the first work of Aristotle in 1497.
sections.rulers:
Venice began as part of the Byzantine Exarchate of Ravenna. After the Lombards conquered most of the exarchate in 751, it was an increasingly autonomous Byzantine outpost. Tradition names Paolo Lucio Anafesto as the first doge in 697, on the authority of a chronicle written about 1008; some modern historians identify him with the exarch Paul. At about the time of the rising of 726 the people of the lagoon elected their own leader, Ursus, the first of 117 doges, whom Byzantium confirmed as dux and hypatus. The ducal seat moved from Malamocco to Rialto under Agnello Particiaco (811 to 827). Charlemagne's son Pepin besieged the lagoon in 810 and failed, and in 814 an agreement between Charlemagne and the Byzantine emperor Nicephorus recognised Venice as Byzantine territory with trading rights on the Adriatic coast.

By the late Middle Ages the city was governed by a Great Council of noble families, which appointed officials and elected a Senate of 200 to 300 members; a Council of Ten controlled much of the administration, and the doge, chosen from the Great Council, usually held office until his death. Under Francesco Foscari (1423 to 1457) the Republic reached its greatest territorial extent. Napoleon conquered Venice on 12 May 1797, and the Austrians took control of the city on 18 January 1798. It joined Napoleon's Kingdom of Italy in 1805, returned to Austria in 1814, and became part of the Kingdom of Italy in 1866, after a revolt under Daniele Manin in 1848 had been crushed in 1849.
sections.life:
The historic city is divided into six districts, the sestieri of Cannaregio, Castello, Dorsoduro, San Marco, San Polo and Santa Croce, created about 1170. They contain parishes, 70 in 1033, reduced under Napoleon and now 38. Each parish chose its patron saint, held its own festivals, gathered round its own market and built its own bell tower. Most Venetians were Roman Catholics, but the state was notable for its freedom from religious fanaticism and executed nobody for heresy during the Counter-Reformation. It was threatened with the interdict several times and twice suffered it, the second time in 1606 under Pope Paul V. The long link with Constantinople left an Orthodox presence, and Armenian merchants from Julfa were leading traders in the 17th century.

The Jews of Venice were compelled to live in the Ghetto. The first complete and uncensored printed edition of the Talmud was printed in Venice by Daniel Bomberg in 1523, and Napoleon, on conquering the city, removed the gates of the Ghetto. Venetian Gothic combined the lancet arch with the ogee arch under Byzantine and Ottoman influence, and the Doge's Palace and the Ca' d'Oro are its chief examples. Early masters of Venetian painting were the Bellini and Vivarini families, followed by Giorgione and Titian, then Tintoretto and Veronese. The glass industry moved to the island of Murano toward the end of the 13th century, and Byzantine craftsmen who fled in 1204 and 1453 helped its development.
sections.crises:
The Black Death devastated Venice in 1348. Plague returned between 1575 and 1577 and killed some 50,000 people in three years; the Festa del Redentore began as thanks for its end. The plague of 1630 killed a third of the city's 150,000 citizens, and the church of Santa Maria della Salute was begun as a thanks offering. Wars wore down the Republic as well. It fought Genoa intermittently from 1350 to 1381 and destroyed the Genoese fleet at Chioggia in 1380. Defeat by the League of Cambrai at Agnadello on 14 May 1509 put French and imperial troops in the Veneto, though Andrea Gritti retook Padua in July and the mainland was recovered after seven years of war.

The Ottoman wars took the eastern possessions. After 1453 Mehmed II began a series of wars; Negroponte fell in 1470, and the peace of 24 January 1479 cost Venice Argos, Negroponte, Lemnos and Scutari and a tribute of 10,000 ducats a year. Famagusta, the last stronghold on Cyprus, surrendered after Turkish attack from 1570, and the Turkish commander had the provveditore Marcantonio Bragadin flayed alive. The Cretan War lasted about 25 years and ended with the surrender of Candia on 6 September 1669. On 12 May 1797 the Great Council voted to hand power to a provisional government by 512 votes to ten with five abstentions, although a quorum was lacking. In the Second World War Jews were rounded up in Venice and deported to extermination camps.
sections.legacy:
The old city and its lagoon were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987. Venice was a centre of printing, painting and music: it was the printing capital of Europe by 1500, and Venetian painting is known for its warm colour scale. Antonio Vivaldi and Tomaso Albinoni were born there, and the Venetian school of music flourished in the 16th century, when Adrian Willaert worked at St Mark's Basilica. Marco Polo (1254 to 1324) and Giacomo Casanova (1725 to 1798) were Venetians. English words from Venetian include arsenal, ghetto, gondola, lagoon, lazaret, lido and regatta.

The city still holds the Venice Biennale, begun in 1895, and the Venice Film Festival, founded in 1932. Buildings from the Republic stand along the Grand Canal, and the Arsenal is still used by the Italian Army. The city also faces flooding. Acqua alta, high water, covers its lowest surfaces; the tide of 13 November 2019 peaked at 1.87 metres, the highest since 1966, and the MOSE barrier was first raised on 3 October 2020. Venice is the capital of the Veneto and of the Metropolitan City of Venice; nearly 50,000 people live in the historic island city and the municipality has about 250,000.

summary: Venice is a city of islands in a lagoon at the head of the Adriatic, traditionally founded in 421. As the capital of a maritime republic it grew rich on trade with Constantinople and the Levant, and, after wars with Genoa and the Ottomans and repeated plague, lost its independence to Napoleon in 1797.
references: John Julius Norwich, A History of Venice (Alfred B. Knopf, 1982)
Gino Benvenuti, Le repubbliche marinare (Newton Compton, 1989)
notes: Founding: the city article gives the dedication of San Giacomo at noon on 25 March 421 as the traditional founding; the history article adds Paduan authorities founding a trading post and says the church dates only from the 11th to mid-12th century. start 421 is marked circa. Neither article gives a firm date.

Doges: the city article puts the first doge Paolo Lucio Anafesto in 697 (tradition) and Ursus as first of 117 doges after the 726 rising; the history article calls Ursus (Orso Ipato) the first doge historically, early in the 8th century, with the first doges' power base at Eraclea, and says Teodato moved the seat to Malamocco in the 740s; the city article says Malamocco was the seat after 751. I kept to the points they share.

Ducal seat to Rialto: city article under Agnello Particiaco (811 to 827); history article c. 810 after Pepin's attack on Malamocco. I wrote 'under Agnello Particiaco (811 to 827)'. The Pax Nicephori is dated 803 in the history article and the agreement 814 in the city article; I gave only 814.
Pepin's siege: both articles give six months and withdrawal; the city article dates it 810.
Treaty of Campo Formio: 12 October 1797 (city article) against 18 October 1797 (history article, Passariano). I left the date out of the text and gave only the treaty.
Counts of islands and bridges differ inside the city article (126 islands and 472 bridges; 118 and 438; 127 islands); left out.
The fleet of 36,000 sailors and 3,300 ships is placed at the peak, late 13th century, in the city article and at 1410 in the history article; the text says so.

The 1630 plague: the city article says a third of 150,000 citizens; the history article says 50,000 died in 16 months, one third of the population. Consistent, so both figures used (a third, of 150,000). The 1575 to 1577 plague: 50,000 in three years (city article); the history article gives a population of 175,000 in 1575 and 124,000 in 1581 (not used).

Famagusta: the city article lists Bragadin as dying in 1571 after the siege; the history article says Famagusta surrendered before Lepanto (7 October 1571) after attack from 1570. I gave no date beyond 'attack from 1570'.

Left out as present-day or guide material: the economy and tourism sections, cruise ships, transport, sport, twin towns, climate, the municipality's government. The population figure of 249,385 is stated 'as of 2026' in the article; I wrote 'about 250,000'. The slave trade is mentioned plainly as the article hedges it ('probably'); the history article's details of the 840 pactum Lotharii, castration houses and slave prices were left out for length and are available if the editor wants them.

Not covered, because the articles give little: the Black Death's death toll in 1348, the Arsenal's workforce, the Rialto market, daily life, women, the Jewish Ghetto's founding date, the 1966 flood's damage.

The Fourth Crusade: both articles say the crusaders and Venetians took Constantinople in 1204; the history article gives the Venetian role (Dandolo, the debt, Zara 1202). Not in the sections beyond the event row; Enrico Dandolo is named only in the city article's notable people list.
